Pick something small, real and shippable in the first week or two, and make sure the path to it is clear. Nothing establishes belonging faster than having done something. A first month of reading documentation and meeting people produces someone who feels like a visitor.

## Structure the first month

- **Week 1** - context, tools, one small task, meeting the immediate team.
- **Week 2-3** - a real piece of work with support, and the wider set of people.
- **Week 4** - working normally, and a check-in on what was confusing.

Name a buddy separate from the manager for the questions people do not want to ask their manager.

## Gotchas

- Write down what "good" looks like at 30, 60 and 90 days, and share it with them on day one. Unstated expectations are the most common cause of an early departure.
- Collect what was confusing at the end of month one and fix it for the next person; the newest person is the only one who can see the gaps.
- Do not schedule the whole first week. Someone with no unstructured time cannot absorb anything.

skills.name: Operational Risk Assessment
skills.description: Identify, score, and mitigate operational risks in a prioritized risk register
skills.whenToUse: Identifying what could go wrong in an operation and deciding what to do about it.
skills.body:
## When to use

Identifying what could go wrong in an operation and deciding what to do about it.

## Enumerate by category, so nothing is forgotten

People (key person, error, fraud), process (failure, gap, control weakness), systems (outage, data loss, security), external (supplier, regulatory, physical), and financial (liquidity, credit, currency). Working through categories finds risks that free association does not.

## Score likelihood and impact separately, on a defined scale

Write the scale down before scoring - what "likely" means in frequency, what each impact band means in currency or in hours of disruption. Undefined scales produce scores that cannot be compared between assessors or over time.

## Decide a treatment for every risk

Avoid, reduce, transfer, or accept. Each with an owner and a date. **Accept** is a legitimate treatment and must be recorded as an explicit decision by someone with the authority to make it - an unrecorded acceptance is just an unmanaged risk.

## Test the controls you are relying on

A risk scored low because a control mitigates it is only low if the control actually works. Where the residual score depends on a control, note when it was last tested. Untested controls are the most common way a risk register is wrong.

## Gotchas

- Single points of failure - one person, one supplier, one system - are systematically under-scored because they have not failed yet.
- Review after every incident, whether or not the incident was on the register. What is missing is the finding.
- A register nobody revisits is a document, not a control.

skills.name: Operational Runbook
skills.description: Turn a recurring task into an exact step-by-step runbook with rollback and escalation
skills.whenToUse: The document someone follows to operate a system - routinely or when it misbehaves.
skills.body:
## When to use

The document someone follows to operate a system - routinely or when it misbehaves.

## Separate routine from exceptional

Two different documents, or two clearly marked sections. Routine operations are read calmly and can carry explanation; exception handling is read under pressure and must be pure procedure. Mixing them means the emergency steps are buried in prose.

## Make every step executable

Exact commands with placeholders clearly marked, the expected output, and what to do if the output differs. Link directly to the dashboards, consoles and logs rather than describing where they are - nobody navigates by description at 3am.

## Include the things people are afraid to write down

- The manual intervention that is technically not supposed to be needed.
- The known flaky step and how many retries is normal.
- What breaks downstream if this is done at the wrong time.
- Who actually knows about this system, by name.

These are the parts that only exist in someone's head, and they are the reason the runbook is worth writing.

## Gotchas

- Test it by having someone unfamiliar execute it; hesitation marks the defects.
- State the blast radius of each destructive step before the step, not after.
- Date it, own it, and review it whenever the system changes. A stale runbook is followed, which makes it worse than none.

skills.name: Overdue invoice collection
skills.description: Draft tone-matched reminders for overdue invoices, scored by payment history
skills.whenToUse: Chasing money that is late, without damaging the relationship.
skills.body:
## When to use

Chasing money that is late, without damaging the relationship.

## Check your own side first

Before chasing, verify: the invoice was actually sent, to the right address and the right entity, with a purchase order number if one is required, and that no dispute or credit note is outstanding. A meaningful share of overdue invoices are overdue because of something on the seller's side, and chasing those costs goodwill for nothing.

## Escalate on a schedule, in a fixed sequence

- **Day 1 past due** - a short, friendly reminder with the invoice attached. Assume it was missed.
- **Day 7** - a call or a direct message to the known contact, asking whether there is a problem with the invoice.
- **Day 14** - escalate to accounts payable and copy the commercial contact, with a statement of all outstanding items.
- **Day 30** - a formal notice referencing the contractual terms, and internal escalation.

The sequence matters more than the wording: predictable, escalating contact collects faster than sporadic chasing.

## Find the actual obstacle

Most late payments are process, not refusal: a missing purchase order, an unapproved invoice, a payment run date, a changed contact. Ask directly what is needed to get it paid and by when, and record the answer.

## Gotchas

- Never threaten anything you will not do, and never mention legal action without authority.
- Get every promise to pay in writing with a date, and diarise the date.
- Repeated late payment from one customer is a credit control decision, not a collections problem.

skills.name: Payroll Cash Check
skills.description: Confirm you can make payroll: forecast cash, rank overdue invoices, stage reminders
skills.whenToUse: Confirming, before the payroll run, that the money will be there and that the run is right.
skills.body:
## When to use

Confirming, before the payroll run, that the money will be there and that the run is right.

## Check the cash first

Payroll is the one payment that cannot be delayed. Confirm the cleared balance on the funding date - not today's balance, and not including receipts expected but not received. Account for the employer taxes and pension payments, which usually leave on a different date and are routinely forgotten in the check.

## Then check the run against last period

Total gross, total net, headcount, and employer cost, each compared with the prior run with every variance explained. A movement with no explanation is an error until proven otherwise. Look specifically at: starters and leavers, contract changes, one-off payments, and anyone whose net moved more than a few percent.

## Check the leavers and the starters individually

These are where errors concentrate. A leaver still on the run, a starter missing, a final payment without the correct accrued leave. Each one is both a cash error and an employee-relations problem.

## Gotchas

- Bank cut-off times and non-working days move the funding date. Count backwards from the pay date using the actual banking calendar.
- Changes to bank details for an employee are a fraud vector; verify out of band, always, and never from the email that requested it.
- Keep the check evidenced. This is a control, not a habit.

skills.name: Process Documentation & SOPs
skills.description: Turn a process in someone's head into an SOP with RACI, steps, and edge cases
skills.whenToUse: Writing down how something is done, so it can be done by someone else, correctly.
skills.body:
## When to use

Writing down how something is done, so it can be done by someone else, correctly.

## Write it while doing it

Documentation written from memory omits exactly the steps that are automatic to the author and unknown to everyone else. Do the process and record each action as you take it, including the ones that feel too obvious to write.

## Structure for the person doing it, not describing it

- **Purpose** - what this achieves and when it is triggered.
- **Prerequisites** - access, tools, information needed before starting.
- **Steps** - numbered, one action each, with the expected result of each.
- **Decision points** - stated as explicit branches.
- **Verification** - how to know it worked.
- **What to do when it goes wrong**, and who to ask.

## Have someone else run it

The only real test. Watch them without helping, and note every hesitation. Every hesitation is a defect in the document, not in the person. Fix them all before publishing.

## Gotchas

- Name a document owner and a review date, both visible on the document.
- Screenshots go stale fastest; use them only where the interface is genuinely ambiguous.
- If the process is so complex it needs a 40-step document, the finding is the process, not the document.

skills.name: Process Optimization
skills.description: Map a workflow, find waste, and design a faster future state with impact
skills.whenToUse: Making an existing process faster or cheaper without breaking what it is for.
skills.body:
## When to use

Making an existing process faster or cheaper without breaking what it is for.

## Measure it before changing it

Map the current process step by step with, for each: who does it, how long it takes, how long it waits before the next step, and how often it is reworked. Wait time between steps is usually the majority of elapsed time and is almost never where people look.

## Attack in this order

1. **Eliminate** - steps that produce nothing anyone uses. Every process accumulates these, usually as a response to an incident that nobody remembers.
2. **Reduce waiting** - batching, handoffs and approvals. Cheaper to fix than the work itself and usually a larger share of the elapsed time.
3. **Simplify** the remaining steps.
4. **Automate** last. Automating a step that should not exist makes it permanent.

## Understand why a control exists before removing it

Every approval and every check was added by someone in response to something. Find out what before removing it. Some are obsolete; some are the only thing preventing an expensive failure, and the difference is not visible from the process map.

## Gotchas

- Measure after the change against the same definition, and include quality and rework, not just speed. Faster with more errors is not an improvement.
- Change one thing at a time or you cannot attribute the effect.
- The people doing the work know where the waste is. Ask them first; it is the cheapest research available.

skills.name: Project Status Report
skills.description: Turn project activity into a leadership-ready report with KPIs, risks, decisions
skills.whenToUse: A recurring report on a project, for people who need to know whether to intervene.
skills.body:
## When to use

A recurring report on a project, for people who need to know whether to intervene.

## Status first, and be honest about it

Green, amber or red, with one sentence of why. The most common failure in status reporting is a project that is green until the week it is red, which means every previous green was wrong and everyone knows it.

A useful rule: if the plan has to go right from here, it is amber.

## Report against the baseline

Scope, date and budget, each against the version everyone agreed. A change to any of the three is a change to report explicitly, with who approved it, not a quiet revision of the baseline.

## Risks and issues, distinguished

A **risk** has not happened yet and has a mitigation and an owner. An **issue** has happened and needs a decision. Conflating them means risks get watched and issues get watched too, when issues need action.

## Gotchas

- Percentage complete is almost always fiction. Report milestones met against milestones planned instead.
- Name the dependency owner when a dependency is late; "waiting on another team" is not a status.
- Keep the format identical week to week so the delta is readable.

skills.name: Quarterly Business Review
skills.description: Build a QBR: revenue and margin trends, customer health, opportunities and risks
skills.whenToUse: Preparing the quarterly review of performance, plans and problems.
skills.body:
## When to use

Preparing the quarterly review of performance, plans and problems.

## Structure it as an argument, not a report

1. **What we said we would do** last quarter.
2. **What happened**, against each commitment - including what did not.
3. **Why**, for the material gaps.
4. **What we are doing about it.**
5. **What we commit to next quarter**, specifically enough to be judged the same way.

A QBR that only reports results without referencing the prior commitments cannot be held to account, which is usually why it is structured that way.

## Be specific about misses

The misses are where the value is. For each: what happened, whether it was a plan problem or an execution problem, what was learned, and what changes. A deck that explains every miss as an external factor is not a review.

## Bring the decisions you need

A QBR with no asks is a status update. List the decisions required, with the options and a recommendation for each, and put them where they will get time rather than at the end.

## Gotchas

- Send the material in advance and use the meeting for discussion. Reading slides aloud wastes the most expensive hour in the quarter.
- Use the same metrics as last quarter, defined the same way.
- Keep the appendix separate; a 60-slide deck with 12 slides of argument reads as evasion.

skills.name: SOX 404 Control Testing Methodology
skills.description: Scope accounts, test control design vs operation, and classify deficiencies
skills.whenToUse: Testing whether an internal control over financial reporting actually operated, to a standard that will survive review.
skills.body:
## When to use

Testing whether an internal control over financial reporting actually operated, to a standard that will survive review.

## Understand the control before testing it

Write down: what risk it addresses, who performs it, how often, what evidence it produces, and what would constitute a failure. A test designed without this tests whatever the evidence happens to show rather than whether the control worked.

## Distinguish design from operating effectiveness

**Design** - would this control, performed as described, prevent or detect the risk? Assess before testing. A well-operated control with a design gap is still a deficiency, and testing operation first wastes the effort.

**Operation** - did it actually happen, every time, for the period?

## Test with evidence, not enquiry

Enquiry alone is not evidence. Rank the methods: re-performance is strongest, then inspection of evidence, then observation, then enquiry. For each item tested record what was inspected, the date, who performed the control, and the conclusion.

## Conclude precisely

Every exception documented with the specific item, what was expected and what was found. Then evaluate: is it an isolated instance or a control failure? Extrapolate the error rate before concluding, rather than after being asked to.

## Gotchas

- An IT-dependent control needs the underlying report tested for completeness and accuracy too, or the test is of a number nobody validated.
- A control performed but not evidenced is a control that failed for testing purposes. Say so.
- Do not test a control that has changed mid-period as one control; it is two populations.

skills.name: SOX Sample Selection & Workpapers
skills.description: Build SOX testing samples, workpaper templates, and control assessments
skills.whenToUse: Selecting a sample for control testing and documenting it so someone else could reach the same conclusion.
skills.body:
## When to use

Selecting a sample for control testing and documenting it so someone else could reach the same conclusion.

## Define the population first, and prove it is complete

The most common workpaper failure is not the sample but the population it came from. Establish the source, the date range, the record count, and evidence that the list is complete - a reconciliation to a system total, not an assertion. An incomplete population invalidates everything downstream.

## Size the sample by frequency and risk

Standard guidance ties sample size to how often the control operates - a handful for a monthly control, more for a daily one, and higher for higher risk. Record the basis for the size chosen rather than the number alone.

## Select in a way that can be re-performed

Random with a documented seed, or systematic with a documented interval and start point. Either way, someone else must be able to reproduce the exact selection. Haphazard selection is not random and does not survive review.

## Write the workpaper to stand alone

Purpose, population and completeness evidence, sample method and size with rationale, the items selected, the test performed on each, the results, the exceptions, and the conclusion. A reviewer should need nothing else and no conversation.

## Gotchas

- If an exception is found, do not quietly extend the sample. Document the exception, then document the decision to extend and why.
- Cross-reference every assertion to its supporting document.
- Sign and date. An unsigned workpaper is not evidence of who did the work.

skills.name: Support ticket triage
skills.description: Categorize a ticket, set P1–P4 priority, check duplicates, and route it
skills.whenToUse: A queue of tickets and the job is to get each to the right place quickly, not to solve them all.
skills.body:
## When to use

A queue of tickets and the job is to get each to the right place quickly, not to solve them all.

## Separate severity from priority

**Severity** is how broken it is. **Priority** is how soon we act, which also weighs who is affected and what is contractually owed. A cosmetic issue for a customer in an escalation can outrank a functional bug for a free user, and conflating the two makes the queue unreadable.

## Triage each ticket into one of four

1. **Answerable now** - answer it and close it.
2. **Known issue** - link to the existing ticket, add the customer, respond with the status.
3. **Needs investigation** - route with the reproduction, the account and the timestamps attached.
4. **Not a support issue** - billing, sales, legal, abuse. Route and tell the customer where it went.

The failure mode is a fifth bucket - things that sit unclassified - so every ticket leaves triage in one of the four.

## Respond even when you cannot resolve

An acknowledgement with a realistic next step resets the customer's clock. Most dissatisfaction with support is about silence rather than about resolution time.

## Gotchas

- Check for a linked existing incident before investigating; parallel investigation of one outage is the most common waste in support.
- Tag the root cause category at close, or the queue can never tell you what to fix.
- A ticket reopened is a ticket that was closed wrongly. Track that rate; it says more than first-response time.

skills.name: Team Capacity Planning
skills.description: Analyze workload and utilization to decide whether to hire, delay, or reprioritize
skills.whenToUse: Working out how much a team can actually take on in a period.
skills.body:
## When to use

Working out how much a team can actually take on in a period.

## Start from available time, not from headcount

Headcount times working days is a fiction. Subtract holiday, public holidays, expected sick leave, meetings, on-call, interviews, and the recurring operational load. What is left is the capacity, and it is routinely 50-65% of the naive number.

## Reserve for the unplanned

Every team has interrupt work - incidents, escalations, urgent requests. Measure the historical share rather than assuming it away, and reserve it explicitly. A plan at 100% of capacity is a plan that fails on the first interruption, and then everything after it is late.

## Plan in ranges

Estimates are uncertain and stating them as points invites them to be treated as commitments. Give a range, and commit to the pessimistic end. A team that consistently delivers its commitment is trusted with more than one that optimistically over-promises.

## Gotchas

- New joiners are negative capacity for their first weeks; someone is onboarding them.
- One person being the only one who can do something is a capacity constraint and a risk. Name it.
- Track actual against planned each period and use the ratio to correct the next plan. Without that feedback the same optimism repeats forever.

skills.name: Vendor Evaluation
skills.description: Evaluate a vendor on cost (TCO), risk, and performance with a recommendation
skills.whenToUse: Evaluating a shortlisted vendor properly, before committing.
skills.body:
## When to use

Evaluating a shortlisted vendor properly, before committing.

## Test against your own case

A scripted demo proves the vendor can drive their own product. Give them your actual scenario, with your data shape and your volume, and watch them do it. Most of what a shortlist misses shows up here: the workflow that needs three tools, the field that does not exist, the export that is not really an export.

## Evaluate the things that outlast the features

- **Support** - hours, response commitment, and what happens at severity one. Ask what their actual median response was last quarter.
- **Roadmap** - and how much of what you need is on it rather than in it.
- **Security and compliance** - the documentation, not the assertion.
- **Data** - who owns it, how you get it out, in what format, and what it costs.
- **Exit** - notice, assistance, and what happens to the data. Negotiate this at the start, when you have leverage.

## Talk to a reference you found yourself

Vendor-supplied references are selected. Find a customer of similar size in a similar sector independently and ask them what went wrong and what they wish they had known. That conversation is worth more than the rest of the evaluation.

## Gotchas

- Cost the integration and the internal effort, not just the licence.
- Check the contract for unilateral price or terms changes before falling in love with the product.
- Score against the criteria written before the demos. Criteria adjusted afterwards describe the winner.

skills.name: Bill negotiation
skills.description: Find retention offers and chat or call your provider to lower a monthly bill
skills.whenToUse: A recurring bill - broadband, mobile, insurance, energy - is higher than it needs to be, and the job is to get it down without losing the service.
skills.body:
## When to use

A recurring bill - broadband, mobile, insurance, energy - is higher than it needs to be, and the job is to get it down without losing the service.

## Know the number before calling

Three things, all findable in ten minutes:

- **What you pay now**, including anything that rolled off a discount.
- **What they charge a new customer** for the same thing today. This is the number that does the work.
- **What a competitor charges**, with the specific plan name.

Also check whether you are in contract and what the exit fee is. Negotiating without that is negotiating blind.

## Ask plainly, once

"My contract has ended and I'm paying £X. You're offering the same package to new customers at £Y, and [competitor] is at £Z. Can you match it?" Then stop talking.

Most first-line agents have a fixed discount they can apply without escalation. If the first answer is no, ask to be put through to retentions or cancellations - that is where the real authority sits, and asking for it directly is normal and expected.

## Be willing to actually leave

The leverage is entirely in being prepared to switch. Know the switching cost and the effort before the call, so that if the answer is no you can say yes to leaving. A threat you would not carry out is read accurately and produces nothing.

## Close it properly

- Get the new price, what it includes, how long it lasts, and any new contract term.
- Get it in writing - email or the account page - before hanging up.
- Diarise the date the discount ends. That date is when this happens again, and forgetting it is how the bill crept up in the first place.

## Gotchas

- A lower price with a longer contract or a worse allowance is not a saving; compare the total over the term.
- Loyalty is not rewarded by default in any of these markets. The discount goes to people who ask.
- Be polite. The person on the phone did not set the price and has discretion they will not use for someone who is rude.
- Never share full card details or a password to "verify"; use the account's own verification.

skills.name: Boolean search sourcing
skills.description: Build precise boolean strings to surface candidates on LinkedIn, GitHub, and more
skills.whenToUse: Finding candidates who are not applying, by searching precisely rather than broadly.
skills.body:
## When to use

Finding candidates who are not applying, by searching precisely rather than broadly.

## Build the query from the work, not the title

Titles are unreliable and vary by company. Search for the evidence of the work: the tools, the certifications, the specific responsibilities. A query built on "Kubernetes AND Terraform AND (SRE OR reliability OR platform)" finds people a title search misses and excludes people a title search wrongly includes.

## Structure it so it can be tuned

```
(title OR synonym OR synonym)
AND (skill AND skill)
AND (location OR remote)
NOT (recruiter OR "seeking opportunities" OR intern)
```

Change one clause at a time and watch the result count. A query changed in three places at once cannot be debugged. Keep the versions that worked.

## Iterate from the results

Read the first twenty profiles. The vocabulary those people use for their own work is better than the vocabulary you guessed - feed it back into the synonym list. This loop is where most of the improvement comes from, not from operator cleverness.

## Gotchas

- Quote multi-word phrases or they are treated as separate terms.
- Different platforms honour different operators; a query that works on one silently degrades on another.
- Exclude your own employees and current candidates before reviewing, not after.
- Boolean finds people who describe their work in writing. That skews by function and by seniority, and it is worth saying so rather than treating the result as the market.

skills.name: Company Policy Lookup
skills.description: Answer plain-language questions about PTO, benefits, travel, and handbook rules
skills.whenToUse: Someone asks what the policy is, and the answer has to be right rather than approximately right.
skills.body:
## When to use

Someone asks what the policy is, and the answer has to be right rather than approximately right.

## Find the authoritative version

There is usually more than one copy and they disagree. Establish which document is authoritative, its effective date and its version, and whether it has been superseded. An answer from an intranet page last edited three years ago is a liability, not an answer.

## Check what varies

The same policy commonly differs by jurisdiction, by employment type, by tenure and by seniority. Confirm which applies to the person asking before answering - a correct answer for the wrong population is a wrong answer.

## Answer with the quote and the source

Give the direct quotation from the policy, then the plain-language reading, then a link to the document and its effective date. Separating the two makes it clear where the policy stops and interpretation starts.

## Gotchas

- Do not interpret where the policy is genuinely silent. Say it is silent and route it to whoever owns the policy - HR, legal, or the manager.
- Policy is not law; local employment law can override it and does.
- If two documents conflict, that is the answer to report, not a problem to resolve by picking one.
- Never answer a policy question about an individual's situation in a way that discloses their circumstances to anyone else.

skills.name: Compensation Analysis
skills.description: Benchmark pay, place against bands, and model equity for offers and retention
skills.whenToUse: Working out what to pay for a role, or whether current pay is defensible.
skills.body:
## When to use

Working out what to pay for a role, or whether current pay is defensible.

## Fix the comparison before looking at numbers

A benchmark is meaningless without: the level, the location or the pay geography, the company size and stage, and the industry. Most disagreements about "market rate" are two people quoting different comparison sets.

## Use more than one source and reconcile them

Survey data, offers you have actually made and lost, and what candidates report. They will disagree; the disagreement is informative. Recent lost offers are the most current signal available and the most under-weighted.

## Compare total compensation, not base

Base, bonus at target, equity with its assumed value and vesting, pension, and anything material in benefits. An equity number without the valuation assumption stated is not a number. Compare like for like or the analysis is decorative.

## Then check internal equity

Before recommending an external number, look inside: does it create an inversion against someone at the same level with more tenure? An offer that fixes a hiring problem and creates three retention problems is a bad trade, and it is the one most often made under time pressure.

## Gotchas

- Survey data lags by six to twelve months in a moving market.
- Self-reported public data over-represents the top of the range.
- Pay transparency legislation may require a published range; check before publishing one that does not match the internal band.
- Document the reasoning. A compensation decision without a written rationale gets relitigated every cycle.

skills.name: Hiring Packet Builder
skills.description: Produce a job post, structured interview guide with rubric, and offer letter from a brief
skills.whenToUse: Assembling everything a hiring decision needs into one document so the decision is made on evidence.
skills.body:
## When to use

Assembling everything a hiring decision needs into one document so the decision is made on evidence.

## What goes in

1. **The role** - the competencies and the bar agreed at kickoff, before anyone was interviewed.
2. **The candidate summary** - background, in three lines.
3. **Per-competency evidence** - the score, the interviewer, and the specific observation supporting it. Quotes, not adjectives.
4. **The concerns**, stated plainly, and what would resolve each.
5. **References**, if taken, and what they added.
6. **The recommendation**, with the reasoning.

## Order it so the bar comes first

The bar written before the interviews, at the top. Reading the evidence first and the bar second is how bars move to fit the candidate in front of you, and that is the single most common failure in hiring.

## Make the disagreement visible

Where interviewers scored differently, show both and say what each saw. A packet that averages the scores into a number hides the most decision-relevant information in the process.

## Gotchas

- Only include what is job-relevant. Personal characteristics, protected or otherwise, do not belong in the packet at all.
- Do not paraphrase an interviewer's concern into something softer; escalate it as written.
- A packet assembled after the decision is a justification. Assemble it before.

skills.name: Org & Headcount Planning
skills.description: Plan headcount, team structure, and hiring sequence with healthy-org benchmarks
skills.whenToUse: Planning what roles to open, when, and what that costs.
skills.body:
## When to use

Planning what roles to open, when, and what that costs.

## Start from the work, not from the org chart

List the outcomes the organisation is committed to next period, and what capacity each needs. Roles that cannot be traced to a committed outcome are aspirations, and they are the ones cut first when the plan meets the budget.

## Model the timing honestly

A role opened in January is not capacity in January. Time to hire plus notice period plus ramp is commonly four to six months for a senior individual contributor and longer for a manager. Plan against the date they are productive, not the date they start - a headcount plan built on start dates over-promises by a quarter.

## Cost fully

Salary, employer taxes, benefits, equity, recruiting cost, equipment, and software seats. Loaded cost is typically well above base, and a plan built on base alone is wrong in the direction that gets noticed later.

## Sequence for dependency

Hire the manager before the team where the team needs managing. Hire the person who defines the work before the people who do it. A plan that hires five juniors into an unmanaged team is a plan to lose them.

## Gotchas

- Include attrition. A plan that assumes nobody leaves is short by the historical rate.
- Distinguish backfill from growth in the plan; they are approved differently and confusing them hides shrinkage.
- State the trigger for each hire. "Open Q2" is a wish; "open when the pipeline sustains X for two consecutive months" is a plan.

skills.name: People Analytics Report
skills.description: Generate headcount, attrition, diversity, or org-health reports from HR data
skills.whenToUse: Reporting on the workforce - headcount, attrition, hiring, distribution - for people who will make decisions from it.
skills.body:
## When to use

Reporting on the workforce - headcount, attrition, hiring, distribution - for people who will make decisions from it.

## Define every metric on the page

Headcount at a point or an average? Does it include contractors? Is attrition voluntary, involuntary or both, and is the denominator the start-of-period headcount or the average? Every one of these choices changes the number materially, and a report that does not state them will be argued with rather than acted on.

## Report attrition as a rate with a cohort view

Annualised rate against the comparable prior period, and separately: voluntary against involuntary, by tenure band, and by function. Attrition concentrated in the first year is a hiring or onboarding problem; attrition concentrated at two years is a progression problem. The single blended number distinguishes neither.

## Be careful with small numbers

Below a threshold - commonly five - a group's figures both mislead and risk identifying individuals. Suppress rather than report, and say that suppression happened rather than leaving a gap.

## Gotchas

- Never report anything that identifies an individual, including by combining two cuts that are each safe alone.
- Distinguish a change in the workforce from a change in how it is recorded; reclassification looks exactly like movement.
- Pair every number with what it would take to change it. A report that only describes is a report that produces a discussion and no action.

skills.name: Performance Review Builder
skills.description: Structure self-assessments, manager reviews, and calibration prep with examples
skills.whenToUse: Preparing a performance review that is specific, evidenced and useful to the person receiving it.
skills.body:
## When to use

Preparing a performance review that is specific, evidenced and useful to the person receiving it.

## Gather the evidence before forming the view

Doing it the other way round produces a narrative and then finds support for it. Collect first: shipped work and its outcomes, peer input, the goals set last cycle and what happened to them, and specific incidents both ways with dates.

## Write against the expectations for the level

Every judgement anchored to the written expectation for their level, not to a comparison with a colleague and not to a general impression. Where there is no written expectation, say so - that is a finding about the framework, and the review should not silently invent one.

## Be specific, and balanced in specificity

The most common failure is precise criticism and vague praise, which reads as criticism throughout. If a concern gets a dated example, so does a strength. Two or three of each is enough; a list of twelve is not read.

## Make the development section actionable

One or two areas, each with what changes, what support is available, and how it will be visible next cycle. "Be more strategic" is not feedback; "own the design for one project end to end, including the stakeholder alignment" is.

## Gotchas

- Recency bias is the dominant distortion. Deliberately review the whole period, especially the first half.
- Nothing in a written review should be a surprise. If it is, that is a management failure to raise it at the time, and it is worth saying so.
- Separate performance from potential and from compensation. Conflating them makes all three conversations worse.

skills.name: Recruiting Pipeline Tracker
skills.description: Track candidates through pipeline stages and the metrics that reveal bottlenecks
skills.whenToUse: Keeping a hiring pipeline in a state where you can tell whether it is going to work.
skills.body:
## When to use

Keeping a hiring pipeline in a state where you can tell whether it is going to work.

## Track the funnel by stage, per role

Applied, screened, first interview, onsite, offer, accepted. Conversion between each. The point is not the totals - it is finding the stage where the rate is unusually low, because that is where the process is broken:

- Low apply-to-screen: the sourcing or the job description.
- Low screen-to-interview: the screen is not selective enough, or the bar is not shared.
- Low onsite-to-offer: the loop is not calibrated, or the role is misspecified.
- Low offer-to-accept: compensation, or the candidate experience during the loop.

## Track time, not just counts

Days in each stage, per candidate. Time in stage is the metric candidates feel, and the best candidates are the ones with other options and the least patience. A candidate sitting six days awaiting scheduling is a candidate being lost quietly.

## Keep the reasons

Rejection reason at every stage, from a fixed list. This is the only data that tells you whether you are rejecting for the right things, and it is the first field to be left blank under pressure.

## Gotchas

- Candidate data is personal data. Retention limits apply, and the tracker is not a place for informal commentary.
- Pipeline totals without a conversion history cannot forecast anything.
- A stalled candidate is not a slow candidate. Chase or close them; leaving them open flatters the pipeline.

skills.name: Structured Interview Kit
skills.description: Design a fair, structured interview: competencies, questions, scorecard, debrief
skills.whenToUse: Building the interview process for a role so that different interviewers reach comparable conclusions.
skills.body:
## When to use

Building the interview process for a role so that different interviewers reach comparable conclusions.

## Start from what the job requires

List the four or five competencies the role actually needs, derived from the work rather than from a template. For each, write what a strong answer demonstrates and what a weak one looks like. If two competencies cannot be distinguished, they are one.

## One competency per interview, one interviewer per competency

Splitting them stops every interview covering the same ground and leaving a gap. Each interviewer knows what they own and is accountable for a verdict on it.

## Write the questions and the rubric together

- Behavioural questions asking for a specific past instance, not a hypothetical.
- Follow-up probes written down, because that is where the signal is.
- A rubric with observable anchors at each level - what a 2 sounds like, what a 4 sounds like. "Strong communicator" is not an anchor; "explained a technical decision to a non-technical stakeholder and named the tradeoff they accepted" is.
- The same questions, in the same order, for every candidate.

## Debrief so the process holds

Independent written scores submitted **before** the discussion. The moment people hear each other first, the loudest voice anchors the room and the structure has bought nothing.

## Gotchas

- Do not add an interviewer to a loop without giving them a competency; an unstructured extra conversation reintroduces exactly the bias the kit removes.
- Consistency includes the take-home: same brief, same time box, same rubric.
- Review the kit against outcomes after a few hires. A competency that never distinguishes anyone is not measuring anything.

skills.name: Competitive Analysis Brief
skills.description: Build a competitive brief: landscape, feature matrix, positioning, win/loss
skills.whenToUse: Understanding a competitor well enough to make a decision, from public information.
skills.body:
## When to use

Understanding a competitor well enough to make a decision, from public information.

## Work from what they publish

Their site, pricing, documentation, changelog, job postings, filings and public statements. Job postings and changelogs are the two most under-read and most informative: postings say what they are building before the site does, and the changelog says what they actually shipped rather than what they announced.

## Establish the shape, not the feature list

- **Who they sell to**, in their own words, and how that has changed.
- **How they charge** - the pricing model matters more than the price, because it says what they think the value metric is.
- **How they sell** - self-serve, sales-led, partner. This determines what they can and cannot respond to quickly.
- **Where they are strong**, honestly.
- **What they do not do**, and whether that looks deliberate.

## Answer the decision

A brief exists to inform a specific decision - how to position, whether to build something, how to respond to a deal. Say what the analysis means for that decision, or the brief is trivia.

## Gotchas

- Only public sources. Anything obtained by misrepresenting who you are is off limits and worthless in a document you might have to disclose.
- A competitor's marketing describes their ambition, not their product. Weight documentation over marketing pages.
- Date everything and re-check quarterly.

skills.name: Contract review & redlining
skills.description: Plain-English contract review with severity-ranked red flags and suggested edits
skills.whenToUse: Reading a contract to find what needs changing, from a commercial rather than a legal standpoint.
skills.body:
## When to use

Reading a contract to find what needs changing, from a commercial rather than a legal standpoint.

## Read for the clauses that bite

In roughly this order:

- **Term, renewal and notice** - auto-renewal with a long notice window is the most common trap.
- **Payment** - amounts, timing, uplift mechanism, and whether uplift is capped.
- **Liability** - the cap, what is excluded from it, and whether it is mutual.
- **Indemnities** - who covers what, and whether it is symmetric.
- **Data** - ownership, processing terms, where it is stored, what happens on exit.
- **Termination** - for convenience, for cause, and what you get back.
- **Change control** - can they change the terms or the price unilaterally?

## Mark each issue by severity

Three levels: cannot sign as written, want changed, and noted. Mixing them means the important redlines get traded away alongside the cosmetic ones. For every "cannot sign", say what would make it acceptable, or the negotiation stalls on a rejection with no path.

## Look for what is missing

Absent clauses are harder to spot than bad ones and often matter more: no SLA, no exit assistance, no cap on uplift, no data return obligation, no subcontractor restriction.

## Gotchas

- This is commercial review, not legal advice. Anything material goes to a qualified lawyer, and that should be stated in the output rather than implied.
- Check the definitions section. A favourable clause can be undone by a definition three pages away.
- Order-of-precedence clauses decide which document wins. Read that before reading the schedules.

skills.name: Cross-tool catch-up digest
skills.description: Daily or weekly digest of action items, decisions, and mentions
skills.whenToUse: Coming back after being away, and needing to know what happened across several systems without reading everything.
skills.body:
## When to use

Coming back after being away, and needing to know what happened across several systems without reading everything.

## Sweep the systems in order of consequence

Not chronologically, and not by tool. In order of what could need action today:

1. Things addressed to you directly and still unanswered.
2. Decisions made in your absence that affect your work.
3. Anything that changed state on work you own - a deal, a ticket, a release, an incident.
4. Everything else, as a count rather than a list.

## Collapse threads to outcomes

A forty-message thread is one line: what was decided and by whom. Reproducing the thread defeats the purpose. Where nothing was decided, say that - an unresolved thread needs you more than a resolved one does.

## Separate needs-you from for-information

Two sections, and the first should be short. The point of a catch-up is to get to action quickly; a single undifferentiated list means reading everything anyway.

## Gotchas

- Respect the boundaries of what you should be reading. A catch-up is not a licence to sweep private channels.
- Note the window covered explicitly, so the gap between the last catch-up and this one is visible.
- Flag anything with a deadline that has already passed at the very top.

skills.name: Customer Question Research
skills.description: Research a customer question across sources with attribution and confidence
skills.whenToUse: A customer has asked something specific and the answer has to be right and traceable.
skills.body:
## When to use

A customer has asked something specific and the answer has to be right and traceable.

## Establish what they are actually asking

Customer questions are usually a symptom. "Does it support SSO" may mean "will our security team approve this". Answer the literal question, and then the underlying one if you can identify it - but do not substitute one for the other.

## Find the authoritative answer

In order: the product itself, then the documentation, then the source, then a person who owns the area. An answer from a colleague's recollection is the least reliable and the most common. Record which source the answer came from.

## Say what is true today, and what is not

- What works now.
- What works with a caveat, and the caveat.
- What does not work, plainly.
- What is planned - only if it is genuinely committed, with no date unless the date is committed too.

Never let "planned" blur into "available". That single ambiguity produces more escalations than any technical limitation.

## Gotchas

- If you cannot verify it, say you will confirm and come back, rather than answering approximately. A wrong answer to a pre-sales question surfaces in month three.
- Keep the answer with its source so the next person does not redo the work.
- Repeated questions are a documentation gap; log them rather than answering them repeatedly.

skills.name: Legal Inquiry Response & Escalation Check
skills.description: Draft responses to common legal inquiries with built-in escalation triggers
skills.whenToUse: An inquiry arrives with legal weight - a complaint, a demand, a regulator's letter - and the first decision is what to do with it.
skills.body:
## When to use

An inquiry arrives with legal weight - a complaint, a demand, a regulator's letter - and the first decision is what to do with it.

## Identify what it is and what clock it started

Many inquiries carry a statutory or contractual deadline, and it usually runs from receipt rather than from when someone noticed. Establish the type, the sender's standing, the deadline, and the consequence of missing it, before anything else.

## Escalate by category, immediately

Escalate on sight, without attempting a response:

- Anything from a regulator, a court, or a law enforcement body.
- A letter before action, or any claim of infringement.
- A data subject request, a breach notification, or anything naming data protection law.
- Anything alleging discrimination, harassment or safety.
- Anything threatening publicity.

For these the only correct first action is acknowledgement of receipt and routing to counsel.

## For the rest, respond carefully

Acknowledge promptly. Answer only what was asked. Do not speculate, do not apologise in terms that admit liability, and do not volunteer information. Have a second person read it before it is sent.

## Gotchas

- Preserve everything the moment an inquiry arrives, including messages and drafts. Deletion after notice is a far worse problem than the original matter.
- Do not forward externally without checking privilege.
- Record the date and channel of receipt. Disputes about deadlines are disputes about that date.

skills.name: Legal Meeting Briefing
skills.description: Prep briefings for legally-relevant meetings and track resulting action items
skills.whenToUse: Preparing someone for a meeting with a legal dimension - a negotiation, a dispute discussion, a regulator.
skills.body:
## When to use

Preparing someone for a meeting with a legal dimension - a negotiation, a dispute discussion, a regulator.

## One page, and it is the position

- **The objective** - what a good outcome is, in one sentence.
- **The position** - what we are asserting, and the basis for it.
- **The fallback** - what we can concede, in what order, and what we cannot.
- **Their likely position**, and the strongest version of their argument. Preparing against the weak version is how meetings go badly.
- **The must-not-says** - anything that would prejudice a position or waive privilege.

## Get the facts and the documents in order

A dated chronology with the source document for each entry, and the two or three documents likely to be referred to, tabbed. Being unable to find a clause in the room costs more than being wrong about it.

## Agree who speaks

Especially where legal and commercial people are both present. An unplanned concession from the commercial side in a legal meeting is the most common way a position is lost.

## Gotchas

- Note explicitly whether the meeting is without prejudice, and whether everyone attending knows what that means.
- Do not brief a position that has not been agreed internally; the meeting is not the place to discover a disagreement.
- Record what was said afterwards, promptly, while it is accurate.

skills.name: Legal Risk Assessment
skills.description: Classify legal risk by severity x likelihood and decide when to escalate
skills.whenToUse: Assessing the legal exposure of a proposed course of action, for a commercial decision-maker.
skills.body:
## When to use

Assessing the legal exposure of a proposed course of action, for a commercial decision-maker.

## Identify the exposures specifically

Not "there is legal risk". Name each one: which obligation, to whom, under what, and what the consequence of breach is - damages, injunction, regulatory penalty, termination right, reputational. A risk that cannot be named cannot be mitigated.

## Score likelihood and impact separately

A near-certain minor breach and an unlikely catastrophic one need different responses and should never be averaged into one score. Impact should include the cost of defending a claim, not only of losing it - that is often the larger number.

## Propose mitigations that are actually available

For each risk: avoid, reduce, transfer (insurance, indemnity, contractual cap), or accept. "Accept" is a legitimate answer and should be written down as a decision with an owner, not left as a silence.

## Gotchas

- This informs a decision; it is not legal advice, and anything material needs a qualified lawyer. Say that in the output.
- Be careful about privilege: an assessment written the wrong way may be disclosable. Route through counsel where that matters.
- Do not soften the language. A risk assessment written to be palatable is a risk assessment that does not work.

skills.name: Legal Team Briefing
skills.description: Daily, topic, or incident briefings synthesized across your legal sources
skills.whenToUse: Preparing a brief for legal so they can advise without a round of clarifying questions.
skills.body:
## When to use

Preparing a brief for legal so they can advise without a round of clarifying questions.

## Lead with the question and the deadline

The single most common failure is a brief that describes a situation without asking anything. State the decision to be made, the specific question, and when the answer is needed. Then the facts.

## Give the facts, all of them

Chronological, dated, and including the unhelpful ones. Legal advice given on a partial picture is worse than none, and the fact left out is usually the one that changes the answer. Attach the documents rather than describing them.

## Separate fact from assumption from inference

Mark each. "The contract auto-renews on 1 March" is a fact if it is in the contract; "we believe they intend to renew" is an inference. Legal will treat them differently and needs to know which is which.

## Say what has already happened

Who has said what to the counterparty, in writing and verbally. Any position already taken constrains the advice, and discovering it afterwards is how advice gets given that cannot be followed.

## Gotchas

- Keep it to what is needed; a brief that buries the question in twelve pages gets read late.
- Flag anything time-critical at the top, not in the body.
- If a document might be privileged or disclosable, say so rather than assuming legal will notice.

skills.name: Multi-source synthesis
skills.description: Merge multi-source results into one cited answer with confidence levels
skills.whenToUse: Several sources on one question, and the job is one coherent answer rather than a summary of each.
skills.body:
## When to use

Several sources on one question, and the job is one coherent answer rather than a summary of each.

## Organise by claim, not by source

A summary of each source in turn is a reading list, not a synthesis. Build the other way round: list the claims, and under each, which sources support it, which contradict it, and how strong each is. The structure of the output is the structure of the disagreement.

## Treat contradiction as the finding

Where sources disagree, do not average them and do not pick the one you like. Work out *why* they disagree - different populations, different definitions, different dates, different incentives. The explanation is usually more valuable than either number.

## Weight before you conclude

Primary over secondary. Recent over old, where the thing changes. Method stated over method absent. Independent over funded by an interested party. Say which weightings you applied, so the reader can disagree with the weighting rather than with the conclusion.

## Write the answer with its confidence

State the conclusion, then how confident you are and why, then what would change it. A synthesis without a stated confidence gets read as certain.

## Gotchas

- Cite at the claim, not at the end. A paragraph with one citation at the end is unverifiable.
- Distinguish "no evidence for" from "evidence against". They are very different findings and are routinely conflated.
- If every source traces to one original, say so - that is one source with an echo.

skills.name: NDA triage
skills.description: Screen an NDA against standard carveouts and classify it green, yellow, or red
skills.whenToUse: An NDA arrives and needs a quick decision: sign, redline, or escalate.
skills.body:
## When to use

An NDA arrives and needs a quick decision: sign, redline, or escalate.

## Check the six things that decide it

1. **Mutual or one-way?** A one-way NDA where you will also disclose is the most common problem.
2. **Definition of confidential information** - is it bounded, and are the standard exclusions present (already known, independently developed, publicly available, required by law)?
3. **Term** - of the agreement and, separately, of the confidentiality obligation. Perpetual obligations on ordinary commercial information are a redline.
4. **Permitted disclosure** - can you tell your own advisers, affiliates and contractors?
5. **Residuals** - a residuals clause substantially weakens the protection; know which side of it you are on.
6. **Governing law and jurisdiction** - a far jurisdiction makes enforcement theoretical.

## Triage to one of three outcomes

- **Standard, sign** - mutual, bounded, standard exclusions, sensible term.
- **Redline** - one or two specific clauses, with the replacement wording ready.
- **Escalate** - non-compete or non-solicit language, IP assignment, anything unusual in the definitions. These are not NDA clauses and their presence in an NDA is the finding.

## Gotchas

- An NDA containing IP assignment or exclusivity is not an NDA. Always escalate.
- Check whether it binds affiliates you cannot actually bind.
- This is triage, not legal advice; anything not clearly standard goes to a lawyer.

skills.name: Source prioritization
skills.description: Order sources by question type and degrade gracefully when one is down
skills.whenToUse: More sources than time, and the job is to read the ones that will change the answer.
skills.body:
## When to use

More sources than time, and the job is to read the ones that will change the answer.

## Rank by what would move the conclusion

Read in the order that could most change what you currently believe. A source that would confirm the working answer is worth less than one that could refute it, and the instinct runs the other way.

## Judge a source before reading it

- **Primary or secondary?** A filing, a dataset, a first-hand account beats an article about one.
- **Who benefits** from this being believed?
- **When** - and does the thing being described change quickly?
- **Method** - for anything quantitative, is the method stated? An unstated method is an unusable number.
- **Independence** - three articles citing one study are one source.

## Stop deliberately

Set the stopping condition up front: when new sources stop changing the answer, or when the remaining questions cannot be settled by reading. Research without a stopping rule expands to fill whatever time exists.

## Gotchas

- The most accessible sources are the most read and therefore the least differentiating.
- A source that everyone cites is often citing something nobody has read. Follow it back once.
- Record what you rejected and why; that list is part of the finding.

skills.name: Regulatory compliance check
skills.description: Map the laws, licenses, and disclosures that apply to a planned action or launch
skills.whenToUse: Establishing whether something is permitted, and what it requires, before it ships.
skills.body:
## When to use

Establishing whether something is permitted, and what it requires, before it ships.

## Scope it before searching

Which jurisdictions, which regulator, which activity, and which date. Regulation is jurisdiction-specific and time-specific, and an answer without both stated is not an answer. If the activity crosses borders, each jurisdiction is a separate question.

## Go to the primary source

The regulation or the regulator's own guidance, not a summary of it. Summaries lag amendments and drop the exceptions, and the exceptions are usually where the answer is. Record the specific provision and its version.

## Separate the three questions

- **Is it permitted?**
- **What must be in place** - registration, disclosure, consent, records, a named responsible person?
- **What must be evidenced**, and for how long? The evidencing requirement is the part most often missed and the part an audit tests.

## Gotchas

- Guidance is not law but regulators enforce against it; note which is which.
- An exemption usually has conditions that must be continuously met, not met once.
- Where the answer is genuinely unclear, say so and recommend qualified advice. A confident wrong answer here is the most expensive kind of output this produces.

skills.name: Research query decomposition
skills.description: Break a question into targeted per-source queries and rank the results
skills.whenToUse: A research question is too broad to answer directly, and the job is to break it into questions that can actually be answered.
skills.body:
## When to use

A research question is too broad to answer directly, and the job is to break it into questions that can actually be answered.

## Split until each part is checkable

Keep splitting until every sub-question has a source that could settle it. "Should we enter the German market" is not answerable; "what is the regulatory requirement for our product category in Germany", "who are the three incumbents and what do they charge", and "what does localisation cost" are.

A sub-question that still needs judgement rather than evidence is not decomposed yet.

## Separate fact from judgement explicitly

Mark each sub-question as one or the other. Facts get sources; judgements get an argument and a named assumption. Mixing them is how a research output becomes an opinion wearing citations.

## Order by what could kill the answer

Do the disqualifying questions first. If the regulatory answer makes the whole thing impossible, nothing else needed doing. Most research effort is wasted by answering the interesting questions before the decisive ones.

## Gotchas

- State what you decided not to investigate, and why. An unexamined branch is a risk the reader should know about.
- If two sub-questions keep collapsing into each other, they are one question and the split was wrong.
- Re-check the decomposition after the first few answers; early findings usually reveal the real question.

skills.name: Session Replay UX Research
skills.description: Analyze session replays to surface user journeys, friction, and pain points
skills.whenToUse: Watching recorded sessions to find where an interface fails people, without leaning on aggregate metrics.
skills.body:
## When to use

Watching recorded sessions to find where an interface fails people, without leaning on aggregate metrics.

## Sample deliberately

Random sessions are mostly uneventful. Sample the ones likely to contain a failure: sessions with a rage click or a rapid back, sessions that abandoned at a known drop-off, sessions unusually long for the task, and sessions from a segment that converts poorly. Then watch a handful of successful ones as a control.

## Watch for hesitation, not just error

The signal is where people slow down: cursor hovering between two options, scrolling up and back down, re-reading, opening a field and leaving it. These are comprehension failures and they never appear in an error log.

## Record observations before interpretations

Note the timestamp, what the user did, and what they appeared to be trying to do - separately from why you think it happened. Interpretation written into the observation cannot be re-examined later.

## Quantify before recommending

A behaviour seen in two sessions is a hypothesis. Check how common it is in the aggregate data before proposing a change; replay finds the problem, analytics sizes it, and a recommendation needs both.

## Gotchas

- Replay tools capture real user data. Confirm that sensitive fields are masked before watching, not after.
- Do not identify individual users in a write-up.
- A session that looks confused may be someone being interrupted. Do not over-read a single recording.

skills.name: Unified cross-tool search
skills.description: One question, parallel searches across chat, email, docs, and trackers
skills.whenToUse: Finding something when you do not remember which system it is in.
skills.body:
## When to use

Finding something when you do not remember which system it is in.

## Search by what you remember, in the right form

People remember fragments: a phrase, a person, a rough date, an attachment. Different systems index different things, so translate the fragment per system - a phrase into full text search, a person into a sender or assignee filter, a date into a range with slack either side because memory of dates is unreliable.

## Search in order of likelihood

Where does this kind of thing usually live? A decision is in chat or a document; a commitment is in email or a ticket; a number is in a sheet or a dashboard. Searching everywhere at once returns noise; searching the likely two systems first usually ends the search.

## Widen deliberately when it fails

- Drop the least certain term first, not the most.
- Try the synonym the other team would use.
- Search for the person rather than the content, then scan their output around the date.
- Look for the thing that referenced it rather than the thing itself.

## Gotchas

- Most search tools stem and stop-word differently; an exact-phrase search that fails may succeed unquoted, and vice versa.
- Archived and deleted items are usually excluded by default and are often where the answer is.
- Only search what you are entitled to see. Finding something you should not have access to is a finding to report, not to use.

skills.name: User research synthesis
skills.description: Cluster interview and survey notes into themes, insights, and recommendations
skills.whenToUse: A set of interviews or sessions, and the job is findings rather than a pile of notes.
skills.body:
## When to use

A set of interviews or sessions, and the job is findings rather than a pile of notes.

## Work from evidence, not from recall

Go back to the transcripts and the recordings. Synthesis from memory reproduces whichever session was most vivid, which is usually the most articulate participant rather than the most representative.

## Code, then cluster

Tag every observation with what it is about, staying close to what was said. Then group the tags into themes. Name each theme as the participants would recognise it, not in your own abstraction - a theme called "cognitive load in onboarding" is a researcher's phrase and loses the specifics.

## Report with counts and quotes

Each finding: how many participants it appeared in, out of how many, and one or two verbatim quotes. The count stops a single strong opinion becoming a finding; the quote stops the finding becoming an abstraction nobody can act on.

## Separate what they did from what they said

Observed behaviour and reported preference are different evidence with different reliability. Where they conflict - and they routinely do - the behaviour is the finding and the conflict itself is worth reporting.

## Gotchas

- Report the disconfirming cases. A finding with no exceptions in a sample of eight is usually a finding about the sample.
- Say how participants were recruited. Recruitment decides what the research can generalise to, and almost nobody states it.
- Do not include personally identifying detail in the write-up.

skills.name: Vendor Agreement Status Check
skills.description: Consolidate a vendor's agreements across systems with gap analysis and deadlines
skills.whenToUse: Establishing where things stand with a vendor agreement - what is signed, what it commits us to, and what is coming up.
skills.body:
## When to use

Establishing where things stand with a vendor agreement - what is signed, what it commits us to, and what is coming up.

## Find the whole agreement

A vendor relationship is rarely one document: a master agreement, an order form, a data processing addendum, a security schedule, and possibly amendments. Assemble all of them and check the order-of-precedence clause, which decides which one wins where they conflict.

## Extract the dates and the money

- Effective date, initial term, current term.
- Renewal mechanism and the notice deadline - with the actual calendar date the notice must be given by.
- Current committed spend, and the uplift mechanism and cap.
- Any minimum commitment and whether it is being met.

## Check obligations both ways

What we owe them (payment terms, usage limits, notification duties) and what they owe us (SLA, support response, security commitments, audit rights). Then check whether either side is actually complying - an unenforced SLA is a discount nobody claimed.

## Gotchas

- Auto-renewal with a 90-day notice window means the decision date is three months before the date everyone has in mind. Put it in a calendar with a reminder.
- An amendment can change the term without changing the master agreement; check for them specifically.
- Note whether the agreement is with the entity that is actually using the service. Group structures make this wrong more often than expected.

skills.name: Vendor shortlisting
skills.description: Turn a vague market need into a short, scored shortlist of vendors, tools, or partners
skills.whenToUse: Narrowing a field of vendors to two or three worth evaluating properly.
skills.body:
## When to use

Narrowing a field of vendors to two or three worth evaluating properly.

## Write the requirements before looking

Split into must-have and nice-to-have, and be honest about which is which. A requirement list written after seeing the options is a list that describes the favourite. Include the non-functional ones - data residency, SSO, uptime commitment, support hours, exit terms - because those are what disqualify late and expensively.

## Disqualify fast, on the cheap criteria

Run the whole field against the must-haves first, using public information only. Anything failing a must-have is out, with the reason recorded. This should remove most of the field in an hour and is the highest-value step in the process.

## Compare the survivors on the same grid

One table, same criteria, same evidence standard. For each cell: the finding and where it came from. Where a vendor's answer is "yes with conditions", record the conditions - that is where the difference usually is.

## Cost the whole thing

Licence, implementation, integration effort, training, and what it costs to leave. A cheaper licence with a heavy integration and a proprietary data format is often the expensive option.

## Gotchas

- A reference the vendor supplies is a reference they chose. Ask for one at your scale and in your sector, and ask them what went wrong.
- Check the security documentation exists before shortlisting; discovering it does not at contract stage costs a month.
- Record why each rejected vendor was rejected. That list is what stops the process restarting when someone new joins the discussion.

skills.name: Account & Prospect Research
skills.description: Research any company or person for sales intel before outreach or a call
skills.whenToUse: Before outreach or a first meeting, establish whether an account is worth the effort and what to lead with.
skills.body:
## When to use

Before outreach or a first meeting, establish whether an account is worth the effort and what to lead with.

## Qualify before you research

Most research effort is spent on accounts that were never a fit. Check fit first - size, sector, geography, and whether they use something you integrate with or replace. If it fails fit, stop and write one line saying why.

## Then build the picture

- **What they sell and to whom.** In their words, from their site.
- **Shape** - headcount, funding, growth direction. Hiring in a function is the clearest signal of investment in it.
- **The trigger** - a raise, a launch, a new executive, a regulation, a public problem. Outreach without a trigger is a cold email with extra steps.
- **The map** - who owns the problem, who signs, who blocks. Name them.
- **Current state** - what they use today for the job you would do.

## What good output looks like

Half a page per account: fit verdict with a reason, the trigger with a date and a link, two named people with roles, and a one-sentence hypothesis of the problem you would solve. Anything longer is not read.

## Gotchas

- Company size from a directory is usually stale and usually high. Cross-check against the careers page or LinkedIn headcount.
- A parent company's news is not the subsidiary's news.
- Record where each fact came from. Half of prospect research is wrong within a quarter and the source is how you tell.

skills.name: CRM activity logging
skills.description: Log calls, emails, and meeting notes into your CRM from inbox and calendar context
skills.whenToUse: Getting what actually happened into the CRM, promptly and consistently enough to be worth querying later.
skills.body:
## When to use

Getting what actually happened into the CRM, promptly and consistently enough to be worth querying later.

## Log the things that are queryable

Free-text notes are unsearchable at scale. The fields that earn their keep:

- **Activity type and date** - call, email, meeting, demo.
- **Contacts involved**, linked rather than typed.
- **Stage change with a reason**, if one happened.
- **Next step and its date.**
- **Loss or risk reason**, from a fixed list rather than prose.

Put the narrative in the note, but never put a fact in the note that belongs in a field.

## Do it same day

Recall degrades within hours and CRM hygiene is entirely a timeliness problem. Same-day partial logging beats complete logging next week, which in practice means never.

## Gotchas

- Match on domain and existing contact records rather than creating new ones; duplicate contacts are how pipeline reporting quietly breaks.
- Do not log a stage change without the evidence that justifies it.
- Auto-captured email and calendar activity is not a substitute for a next step, which no integration can infer.

skills.name: CRM Cleanup Pass
skills.description: Find stale deals, duplicate contacts, and missing fields in your CRM, then fix them
skills.whenToUse: The CRM has decayed to the point where reports are not trusted. A structured pass to make it queryable again.
skills.body:
## When to use

The CRM has decayed to the point where reports are not trusted. A structured pass to make it queryable again.

## Fix in this order

Later steps depend on earlier ones, so the order matters:

1. **Duplicates** - merge accounts by domain, then contacts by email. Doing anything else first means doing it twice.
2. **Ownership** - unowned or ex-employee-owned records, reassigned or archived.
3. **Stage and close date integrity** - anything with a close date in the past is either closed or wrongly dated. There is no third option.
4. **Required fields** on open opportunities - amount, stage, next step.
5. **Stale records** - no activity beyond a defined threshold, closed out with a reason rather than deleted.

## Decide the rules before you start

Write down what counts as a duplicate, what counts as stale, and which record wins in a merge. Applying a rule you invented halfway through is how a cleanup becomes its own data-quality incident.

## Gotchas

- Export everything before the first write. Merges are not reversible in most CRMs.
- Work in batches with a spot-check between them, not one bulk operation.
- Closing a stale deal changes historical win rate. Note the date of the cleanup so the discontinuity in the reporting is explainable.
- Cleanup without a change to how records are created just buys a few months.

skills.name: Daily Sales Briefing
skills.description: Start the day with a prioritized brief: meetings, pipeline alerts, and emails
skills.whenToUse: The first ten minutes of the day: what changed overnight and what needs action before lunch.
skills.body:
## When to use

The first ten minutes of the day: what changed overnight and what needs action before lunch.

## What goes in

In priority order, and nothing else:

1. **Replies waiting on you**, oldest first, with the thread's last line quoted.
2. **Deals with a date this week** - a close date, a renewal, a contract expiry.
3. **Deals that went quiet** past their normal cadence, with days since last contact.
4. **Today's meetings**, each with the one fact you need going in.
5. **Account signals overnight** - a news item, a product usage change, a support escalation on an open deal.

## Rules that keep it useful

- Cap it. A briefing longer than one screen gets skimmed and then ignored.
- Every item has a next action, or it is information and belongs at the bottom.
- Sort by what decays fastest, not by deal size.
- If nothing needs action, say so. A briefing that manufactures urgency daily stops being read.

## Gotchas

- Timezones: "overnight" is different for a rep in a different region. Anchor to the reader's local day.
- A deal is not quiet because the CRM was not updated. Check the inbox before flagging silence.
- Do not include forecast maths here. That is a weekly exercise and it distracts from the calls.

skills.name: Lead Triage & Call List
skills.description: Score inbound leads by engagement, fit, and urgency into a ranked call list
skills.whenToUse: A pile of inbound or list-sourced leads and limited hours. The job is an ordered call list, not a scored spreadsheet.
skills.body:
## When to use

A pile of inbound or list-sourced leads and limited hours. The job is an ordered call list, not a scored spreadsheet.

## Rank on two axes only

**Fit** - do they look like the customers who succeed? **Intent** - is there evidence they are in motion right now?

Intent beats fit for ordering today's calls: a mediocre-fit lead who requested a demo this morning is a better call than a perfect-fit lead who downloaded a PDF last quarter. Fit decides whether they stay on the list; intent decides the order.

## Signals worth weighting

- Demo or pricing page request - highest, and decays within days.
- Multiple people from the same domain in a short window - a buying group forming.
- Reply to an earlier sequence, even a negative one.
- A trigger event at the account.
- Job title matching the economic buyer rather than an end user.

## Produce the list

One row per lead, ordered, with: name, company, why now (the specific signal and its date), the opening line, and the next step if they do not answer. Cap it at what can genuinely be called today - a list of 200 is a list nobody works.

## Gotchas

- Deduplicate by domain, not by email. Three people from one company is one account.
- Route rather than discard poor-fit leads with real intent; they are often referrals waiting to happen.
- Freshness decays fast. A list built on Monday is a different list by Thursday, so rebuild rather than work down.

skills.name: Personalized Outreach Drafting
skills.description: Research a prospect, then draft personalized cold email and LinkedIn outreach
skills.whenToUse: Writing outreach that gets a reply, at more than one-at-a-time volume, without it reading as generated.
skills.body:
## When to use

Writing outreach that gets a reply, at more than one-at-a-time volume, without it reading as generated.

## The structure that works

Four sentences, in this order:

1. **The specific reason for writing** - the trigger, named, with enough detail that it could only be about them.
